notes: Asylum credibility judicial review; IAT refusal upheld despite adjudicator error on PTSD analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Burundi asylum credibility and PTSD medical evidence
key_facts: The claimant, a minor Burundi national, claimed asylum after alleged village attack, parental deaths and rape in April 2002.
An adjudicator dismissed her appeal on credibility grounds, including discrepancies over hidden money and a photograph or pendant.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal.
Dr Eastgate diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder, but the adjudicator treated the diagnosis as dependent on accepting her account.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal against an adjudicator's asylum dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review application dismissed; permission had been granted but the claim failed on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: Even where an adjudicator erred in treating a PTSD diagnosis as necessarily wrong because the asylum account was disbelieved, that error was not determinative where substantial independent credibility findings—interpretation discrepancies, English language ability, and the plausibility of the escape journey—justified disbelief of the claim.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator and IAT properly considered complaints about interview interpretation
Weight to be given to medical evidence of PTSD where credibility is in issue
Whether supporting evidence including a birth certificate outweighed adverse credibility findings
Whether the IAT erred in refusing leave to appeal

confidence.notes: Outcome, credibility reasoning and limited PTSD error finding are explicit. Source metadata lists no judges.

notes: Self-employed retirement annuity vesting in bankruptcy; HRA retrospectivity and Article 14 analysis are detailed and conclusive.

enrichment.short_title: Bankrupt's retirement annuity and Article 14 pension discrimination
key_facts: Mr Malcolm took out a retirement annuity contract in 1986 as a self-employed graphic designer and was made bankrupt in 1996.
His trustee sought to realise the pension contract after Re Landau and Krasner v Dennison held such benefits vested in the trustee.
Section 11 of the Welfare Reform and Pensions Act 1999 exempted approved pension rights from bankruptcy estates but only for petitions presented after 29 May 2000.
Mr Malcolm argued the trustee had no interest in the pension and that differential treatment of self-employed and occupational pension holders breached Article 14 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in bankruptcy proceedings challenging the trustee's entitlement to the retirement annuity and raising Human Rights Act incompatibility arguments.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; trustee entitled to realise the retirement annuity under pre-1999 law and Mr Malcolm could not rely on Convention rights for pre-October 2000 acts.
enrichment.ratio: A self-employed holder's retirement annuity contract vested in the trustee in bankruptcy under the Insolvency Act 1986 before the 1999 reforms; the Human Rights Act 1998 did not permit complaint of pre-commencement acts in the bankrupt's own application, and Article 14 did not make unlawful the trustee's mandatory realisation of contract-based pension benefits where the comparator involved trust-based occupational schemes with forfeiture clauses.
legal_issues: Whether the trustee was entitled to the retirement annuity contract
Whether section 11 Welfare Reform and Pensions Act 1999 applied retrospectively
Retrospective effect of section 22(4) Human Rights Act 1998 in bankruptcy applications
Whether differential bankruptcy treatment of retirement annuities and occupational pensions was Article 14 discrimination
linked_authorities: Re Landau [1998] Ch 223
Krasner v Dennison [2001] Ch 76
Rowe v Saunders [2002] EWCA Civ 242
Wilson v First County Trust Ltd (No. 2) [2003] UKHL 40
Wandsworth Borough Council v Michalak [2002] EWCA Civ 271
Kemble v Hicks [1998] PLR 141

confidence.notes: Dismissal, statutory timeline and HRA retrospectivity analysis are clearly reasoned despite length.

notes: Leading self-assessment discovery appeal; Court of Appeal restored section 29 assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Self-assessment discovery assessment and section 29(5) TMA
key_facts: Mr Veltema's 1997/98 self-assessment declared a £100,000 benefit-in-kind from his company transferring a house to him.
The enquiry period expired on 31 January 2000 before the Revenue discovered the open market value was about £145,000.
The Inspector raised a £18,000 discovery assessment under section 29 Taxes Management Act 1970.
General Commissioners and Park J held section 29(5) was not satisfied because the Inspector should have investigated further.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the General Commissioners' allowance of the taxpayer's appeal against a section 29 discovery assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 29 assessment of £18,000 restored with costs orders varied.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 29(5) TMA the test is whether the officer could not have been reasonably expected to be aware of an actual insufficiency in the assessment, not merely a possible undervaluation warranting further checks; section 29(6) confines the relevant information principally to that emanating from the taxpayer, and on the facts neither the return nor the P11D indicated the valuation was unreliable.
legal_issues: Whether section 29(5) requires awareness of actual insufficiency or possible insufficiency
Whether enquiries an officer could reasonably have been expected to make are part of the section 29(5) test
Whether section 29(6) exhaustively defines information made available to the officer
Whether the P11D form was relevant information for section 29(5)
linked_authorities: Cenlon Finance Co Ltd v Ellwood (1961) 40 TC 176
Scorer v Olin Energy (1985) 58 TC 592

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, unanimous outcome and restored assessment are explicit.

notes: Planning ancillary use challenge; Harrods approach applied and JR dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Helicopter museum ancillary flights and planning enforcement

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: The International Helicopter Museum at Weston-super-Mare had planning permission for museum use only, subject to a restricting condition.
Helicopter experience flights and visitor helicopter flights increased significantly from the mid-1990s, causing noise complaints from adjoining business park tenants.
The council decided at present levels those flights were ancillary to museum use and declined enforcement action.
The claimant sought judicial review of council decisions on 5 February and 8 October 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Linked claims for judicial review of local planning authority decisions not to take enforcement action against helicopter flights at a museum.
enrichment.ratio: At present levels, helicopter experience flights and visitor flights linked to museum attendance may, as a matter of fact and degree, be reasonably incidental to museum use rather than a material change of use requiring separate permission; the council's approach was consistent with Harrods and not Wednesbury unreasonable, with monitoring reserved for future intensification.
legal_issues: Whether helicopter flights were ancillary to permitted museum use or a material change of use
Application of the Harrods approach to ancillary activities
Whether the council asked the correct legal question
Whether the council's decision was Wednesbury unreasonable
linked_authorities: Harrods Ltd v Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions [2002] JPL 1258

confidence.notes: Dismissal, ancillary-use reasoning and monitoring condition are clearly stated.

notes: Long TCC trial on IT services contract termination; £700,000 debt judgment clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Peregrine IT software contract wrongful termination debt
key_facts: Peregrine Systems supplied ServiceCenter call-centre software and related services to Steria under a software licence and services agreement.
Steria terminated the agreement by letter dated 5 February 2003 alleging Peregrine breaches including training, implementation and ROI failures.
Peregrine claimed £700,000 due on 28 February 2003 for licensed products, maintenance and professional services.
Steria counterclaimed for repayment of sums paid and damages for alleged misrepresentation and breach.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of liability and quantum following alleged contractual termination of an IT software and services agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Peregrine in the sum of £700,000 with contractual interest from 28 February 2003; Steria's termination and counterclaims failed.
enrichment.ratio: Steria was not entitled to terminate under clause 7(b)(i) or at common law for repudiatory breach because Peregrine had not breached the obligations relied on; the £700,000 fell due before the agreement was terminated and was recoverable as a debt notwithstanding limitation-of-liability clauses relevant only to damages claims.
legal_issues: Whether Steria was entitled to terminate for alleged breaches of training, implementation and ROI obligations
Construction of termination clauses and repudiatory breach
Whether £700,000 was due as a debt before termination
Effect of limitation and exclusion clauses on the quantum claim

notes: Section 78 voire dire on pre-interview disclosure; appeal dismissed with guidance on Mason.

enrichment.short_title: Robbery appeal and pre-interview police disclosure
key_facts: Mr Farrell was convicted of robbery and attempted robbery and sentenced to concurrent ten-year terms based largely on circumstantial links to getaway vehicles.
In a pre-interview disclosure document the police did not mention false number plates on a hired Ford Focus or wider offences they intended to question him about.
Farrell told lies in interview about lending the car; the judge gave a Lucas direction and admitted the interview under section 78 PACE.
The interviewing officer acknowledged limiting disclosure to avoid an immediate no-comment interview.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction following a voire dire ruling admitting a police interview despite alleged incomplete pre-interview disclosure.
enrichment.ratio: Incomplete pre-interview disclosure does not necessarily render an interview unfair under section 78 PACE; omission of further offences or withheld details such as false plates is distinguishable from deliberate deceit in R v Mason, and the trial judge was entitled to find no impropriety or relevant prejudice where the defendant told lies rather than admissions induced by non-disclosure.
legal_issues: Whether police must disclose all known facts before interview
Application of R v Mason to non-disclosure tactics
Exercise of discretion under section 78 PACE
Whether denial of a no-comment interview caused relevant prejudice
linked_authorities: R v Mason (1987) 86 Cr App R 349
R v Roble [1997] Crim LR 449
R v Jamieson and McDonagh [2003] EWCA Crim 3755

confidence.notes: Dismissal and section 78 reasoning are explicit; court declined to lay down fixed disclosure rules.

notes: Complex reinsurance section 69 appeal; source full_text appears truncated before formal order though first-ground reasoning favours Lincoln.

enrichment.short_title: Reinsurance net retained lines and prior arbitration award
key_facts: Lincoln reinsured Sun/Phoenix under a whole-account layer containing a net retained lines clause.
Unicover whole account reinsurances were initially protected by Lincoln but Sun/Phoenix also sought cover under Cigna occ/acc reinsurances placed orally in August 1998.
Cigna arbitrators avoided the Cigna reinsurance for misrepresentation but found Unicover risks would otherwise have been covered.
Lincoln arbitrators held Lincoln must indemnify Sun/Phoenix for Unicover losses; Lincoln appealed under section 69.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court appeal under section 69 Arbitration Act 1996 against an interim final award on reinsurance indemnity and net retained lines, with a section 68 serious irregularity challenge.
enrichment.outcome: On the first ground of appeal, Lincoln was entitled to succeed because the Cigna award determined Unicover risks were reinsured by Cigna subject to avoidance, triggering the net retained lines exclusion; second ground and section 68 challenge rejected in the reasoning.
enrichment.ratio: Where a reinsurer's liability under a net retained lines clause depends on whether losses would have been recoverable from another reinsurer, findings in a reasoned prior arbitration between the reinsured and that reinsurer on scope of cover may bind the parties in later proceedings even though the stranger reinsurer was not a party, and the Lincoln tribunal erred in departing from the Cigna arbitrators' determination that Unicover whole account risks were covered by Cigna.
legal_issues: Whether Lincoln arbitrators were bound by the Cigna arbitration award on scope of cover
Construction of a net retained lines clause where the other reinsurance was avoided
Effect of Hollington v Hewthorn on subsequent arbitration proceedings
Whether coverage could be found partly in an oral agreement contrary to slip market practice

enrichment.short_title: Circular saw bench injury and work equipment regulations

statutes_considered.title: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998
Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mr Sherlock, an experienced joiner employed by Chester City Council, lost his thumb and index finger using a portable bench circular saw in January 2000.
The council provided the saw after a request to speed fascia trimming but carried out no risk assessment, training or run-off bench provision.
Long 5-metre fascia boards tended to bow unless supported by a second worker or run-off bench.
The trial judge dismissed the claim, finding the accident was entirely the claimant's fault.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court trial dismissing an employer's liability claim for a workplace circular saw injury.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment for the appellant with contributory negligence assessed at 60%, remitted for assessment of damages.
enrichment.ratio: An employer's failure to carry out even an informal risk assessment and to instruct an experienced employee to use a run-off bench or second person when cutting long flexible boards breached the common law duty and Regulations 8 and 20; that fault was causative and not co-extensive with the employee's conscious acceptance of an obvious risk, though the skilled employee bore greater responsibility.
legal_issues: Whether lack of run-off bench support caused the accident
Causation of admitted breaches of work equipment regulations
Application of Ginty v Belmont Building Ltd where employee knew the precaution
Apportionment of contributory negligence in statutory duty cases

key_facts: Mr Perotti has litigated for years over the estate of his uncle Lorenzo Perotti, including a 1997 administration action against solicitor administrator Mr Watson.
Neuberger J made an extended civil restraint order on 10 April 2003 after repeated Grepe v Loam orders.
Park J appointed Mr Watson administrator de bonis non under section 116 in October 2003, refusing a grant to Mr Perotti.
Chadwick LJ refused ten permission to appeal applications and related review applications in February 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice determination of multiple applications for permission to appeal and one CPR 52.16(6) review in long-running estate litigation.
enrichment.outcome: All applications for permission to appeal refused; limited temporary stay of sale of 43A Ridgmount Gardens until disposal of a separate Lindsay J permission application; further appellant's notices not accepted until March 2004 hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Decisions refusing adjournments of civil restraint applications and appointing a creditor-administrator under section 116 involve exercises of discretion not open to interference where ample grounds supported an extended restraint order; serial meritless permission applications defeat the purpose of such orders unless further appeal restrictions are considered.

key_facts: The claimant sought judicial review of an immigration decision certified under section 94 Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

The claimant argued it was irrational to include Bangladesh in the section 94 country list, citing Javed on Pakistan.

enrichment.ratio: Where a renewed permission application raises an arguable challenge to the lawfulness of listing Bangladesh under section 94, following the Court of Appeal's approach in Javed albeit potentially distinguishable, a substantive hearing is appropriate to give authoritative guidance on the point.
